ticks.label: 1600 AD
ticks.name: Before Westphalia
ticks.narrative: In 1600 Europe’s great powers are composite monarchies and trading republics: Spanish Habsburgs still claim a global monarchy; the United Provinces prove a rebel republic can win; Bourbon France stabilizes after civil war; England and Scotland remain dynastically separate under one Stuart prospect. The Holy Roman Empire’s confessional truce is fragile; Sweden and Poland eye the Baltic; Muscovy reels in the Time of Troubles. This is the map on which the Thirty Years’ War will detonate.

ticks.label: 1648 AD
ticks.name: Peace of Westphalia
ticks.narrative: 1648 ends the Thirty Years’ War and the Eighty Years’ War: Westphalia and Münster recognize Dutch and Swiss independence, freeze a confessional patchwork inside the Empire, and elevate France and Sweden as guarantors. Spain is weakened; the Empire’s emperor is more Austrian dynast than universal lord; Brandenburg gains ground toward Prussia. England’s civil wars remake the British Isles offstage. ‘Westphalian’ sovereignty is born as settlement, not ideology slogan.

ticks.label: 1700 AD
ticks.name: Spanish Succession threshold
ticks.era: Louis XIV, Northern War, Peter’s Russia
ticks.narrative: Around 1700 Louis XIV’s France is the continental yardstick as the Spanish Habsburg line dies out, triggering the War of the Spanish Succession. Sweden’s Carolines still fight the Great Northern War against Peter the Great’s rising Russia and its allies; the Dutch Republic peaks then strains; England and Scotland are months from the 1707 Union. Ottomans have lost Hungary to the Habsburgs after 1699 — the eastern question is already imperial competition.

ticks.label: 1750 AD
ticks.name: Enlightenment great-power concert
ticks.narrative: By 1750 Prussia under Frederick II is a military great power; Britain (after 1707) contests France for colonial primacy; Austria’s Habsburgs regroup after succession wars; Russia is a European player. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth weakens toward partition; the Dutch decline as financiers more than generals; Enlightenment salons and academies redefine elite culture. The Diplomatic Revolution will soon realign Austria with France against Prussia and Britain — Seven Years’ War soon.

ticks.label: 1789 AD
ticks.name: Eve of the French Revolution
ticks.era: Partitions of Poland, ancien régime crisis
ticks.narrative: In 1789 Bourbon France collapses into revolution while Europe’s map still shows absolute and composite monarchies: Britain’s fiscal-military state, Joseph II’s reforming Austria, Frederick William’s Prussia, Catherine’s Russia, and a thrice-partition-bound Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (first cut 1772). The Holy Roman Empire is a hollow constitutional shell; Ottomans retreat in the Balkans. Industrial and Atlantic revolutions are underway — the nation-state map of the next century is not yet drawn.

narrative: From the Dutch Revolt’s consolidation and the Thirty Years’ War through Westphalia, Bourbon–Habsburg rivalry, Sweden’s Baltic rise and fall, Russia’s empire, Ottoman retreat from Hungary, Prussian ascent, and the First Partition of Poland—Europe’s map on the eve of the French Revolution is a system of composite monarchies and commercial republics, not nation-states.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.description: From Henry IV’s peacemaking after the Wars of Religion to Louis XIV’s Versailles machine, Bourbon France forges the template early modern state: intendants, standing army, mercantilist navy, and a sacral kingship that claims Gallican control of the church. Treaties of Westphalia, the Pyrenees, Nijmegen, and Utrecht push the frontier toward a recognizable hexagon; Lorraine (1766) and Corsica (1768) close the pre-revolutionary outline. By 1789 the Old Regime still rules a nearly modern territorial kingdom—rich, centralized, and fiscally brittle—on the eve of revolution. Henry IV’s ‘chicken in every pot’ peace gives way to Richelieu’s state reason; Louis XIV’s sun-king theatre of power peaks at Nijmegen then overreaches into endless coalition war.
polities.conflicts: Richelieu’s interventions in the Thirty Years’ War; Franco-Spanish War (1635–59); Dutch War (1672–78); Nine Years’ War / War of the League of Augsburg; War of the Spanish Succession; War of the Polish Succession; War of the Austrian Succession; Seven Years’ War (global defeat); American Revolutionary War alliance (1780s). Domestic hinges: sieges of La Rochelle, the Fronde, dragonnades after the Revocation of Nantes.
polities.leaders: Henry IV; Louis XIII with Cardinal Richelieu; Anne of Austria & Mazarin; Louis XIV with Colbert and Louvois; Louis XV with Fleury and Choiseul; Louis XVI. Military and diplomatic foils: Condé, Turenne, Vauban, Vergennes.
polities.religion: Catholic monarchy with a Gallican church claiming liberties against Rome. Edict of Nantes (1598) licenses Huguenot coexistence until Louis XIV’s Revocation (Fontainebleau, 1685) drives a skilled Protestant diaspora to the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg, and Switzerland. Jansenist controversies and later philosophe anticlericalism erode confessional certainties without yet ending the sacral kingship of the Most Christian King.
polities.culture: Versailles invents court society as political theatre—etiquette, ballet, and French as the language of European elites. Académies (Française, Sciences, Peinture) standardize taste and inquiry; Paris salons and provincial academies circulate novels, encyclopedias, and reform talk. Culinary, fashion, and print industries make French style an export commodity as much as wine or silk.
polities.summary: Bourbon absolutist kingdom that sets Europe’s court language, fiscal-military model, and Enlightenment quarrel with itself.
polities.story: Richelieu’s siege of La Rochelle (1627–28) breaks armed Huguenot autonomy and announces that sovereignty will no longer share forts with confessions. A generation later, Louis XIV’s personal rule after 1661 turns that lesson into architecture: the Hall of Mirrors, the war ministry, and the Revocation’s refugees. The Seven Years’ War strips overseas primacy to Britain; debt and privilege then carry the crisis into 1789, when the Estates-General open and the kingdom’s map still looks ‘complete’ while its politics implode.
polities.literature: Corneille and Racine refine classical tragedy; Molière anatomizes hypocrisy; La Fontaine’s fables and Pascal’s Pensées braid wit with Augustinian dread. The eighteenth century shifts to Voltaire’s pamphlets, Montesquieu’s Spirit of the Laws, Rousseau’s Social Contract and Confessions, Diderot’s Encyclopédie, and Laclos’s dangerous drawing rooms—letters as weapons against privilege.
polities.art: Poussin and Claude invent a French classical landscape of reason; Le Brun and the Gobelins manufacture Louis XIV’s visual ideology; Watteau’s fêtes galantes and later Boucher/Fragonard rococo soften the court. David’s oath-taking neoclassicism (1780s) already paints republican virtue under a still-reigning king. Dress—justaucorps, powdered wigs, later simpler anglomanie—broadcasts rank before words do.
polities.ideas: Descartes’s method and dualism, then Malebranche and Bayle’s critical dictionary, set a French path from scholasticism to systematic doubt. Montesquieu’s separation of powers and Voltaire’s anticlerical campaign export a reform vocabulary across Europe; Rousseau’s general will and inequality discourses radicalize it. Physiocrats (Quesnay) theorize land as wealth while Colbertist habits still run the ministries.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.description: England enters the century in personal union with Scotland (1603) yet keeps its own parliament, law, and church. Civil wars, regicide, Commonwealth, and Restoration remake the constitution; the Glorious Revolution and Bill of Rights (1689) bind the crown to Protestant parliamentary consent. Mapped separately until the 1707 union folds it into Great Britain. Overseas, chartered companies and Navigation Acts hitch domestic politics to Atlantic and Asian trade. A king who believes in divine right meets a Parliament that controls the purse—civil war follows, a king is tried and executed (1649), and a republic briefly rules.
polities.conflicts: Aid to the Dutch Revolt; Bishops’ Wars with Scotland; Wars of the Three Kingdoms / Civil Wars (1642–51); Anglo-Dutch Wars; Nine Years’ War; opening of the War of the Spanish Succession. Domestic violence includes the Irish campaigns under Cromwell and Monmouth’s rebellion (1685).
polities.leaders: Elizabeth I (century’s edge); James I; Charles I; Oliver Cromwell & the Protectorate; Charles II; James II; William III & Mary II; Anne. Thinkers-in-power: Shaftesbury’s Whigs, Clarendon, Godolphin, Marlborough.
polities.religion: Established Church of England under royal supremacy, pressed by Puritan reform and Catholic fear. Civil War sects (Independents, Baptists, Quakers) explode under the Commonwealth; Restoration reimposes Anglican uniformity; Toleration Act (1689) eases Trinitarian Protestant dissenters while Catholics and Unitarians stay disabled.
polities.culture: Jacobean and Caroline letters give way to Restoration theatre, coffee-house news culture, and a London that becomes Europe’s financial and print capital after 1688. Common law, county militias, and parish governance keep the state surprisingly local even as the navy goes global.
polities.summary: Stuart England wrestles crown and parliament into civil war, Commonwealth, Restoration, and the 1688 settlement before the 1707 union.
polities.story: Charles I’s scaffold (1649) proves a European king can be tried by his subjects; Cromwell’s Protectorate then shows how hard it is to invent a republic without an army. 1660 restores the crown but not divine-right ease; 1688–89 settles the fight by importing William of Orange and writing limits into statute. Newton’s Principia (1687) lands in the same decade as the Bill of Rights—order in cosmos and constitution.
polities.literature: Shakespeare’s late afterglow; Donne and the metaphysical poets; Milton’s Paradise Lost after regicide; Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress from a dissenting jail; Dryden’s public verse; Aphra Behn’s stage and novels; early periodical essays that teach a reading public how to argue politics in prose.
polities.art: Van Dyck’s courtly Stuart portraits; Puritan distrust of images in churches; Wren’s rebuilt London skyline after the 1666 Fire; Lely and Kneller’s Restoration and Williamite faces. Costume moves from ruff and doublet toward periwig and justaucorps under French influence, then English practicality.
polities.ideas: Hobbes’s Leviathan answers civil war with absolute sovereignty; Locke’s Two Treatises and Letter on Toleration answer 1688 with consent, property, and limited government. Harrington, the Levellers, and later Commonwealthmen keep republican arguments alive in pamphlets even when kings return.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.description: Scotland keeps separate law, kirk, and parliament after James VI inherits England (1603). Covenanting resistance to Charles I’s prayer book detonates the Wars of the Three Kingdoms; later Stuart restorations and Williamite settlement leave a Presbyterian establishment uneasy with Jacobite Highlands. The 1707 Act of Union ends separate statehood on this map while preserving Scots law and the Kirk. James VI leaves for London in 1603 wearing two crowns; Scotland keeps its parliament and kirk until bishops and prayer books light the Covenant.
polities.conflicts: Bishops’ Wars (1639–40); Wars of the Three Kingdoms; Cromwellian occupation; Glencoe (1692) as Williamite coercion; Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 fall after the map’s Scottish layer ends. Darien Scheme’s failure (1690s) softens elite resistance to union.
polities.leaders: James VI/I; Charles I; Covenanter regimes and Argyll; Charles II; James VII/II; William II (III of England); Anne. Union negotiators and Darien backers frame the endgame.
polities.religion: Presbyterian Kirk dominant after Reformation; episcopal experiments under Charles I and after Restoration provoke revolt and the Killing Time. Post-1689 Presbyterian settlement; Episcopalians and Catholics persist as minorities, especially in the northeast and Highlands.
polities.culture: Gaelic Highlands and Scots-speaking Lowlands under one crown; universities at St Andrews, Glasgow, Aberdeen, and Edinburgh feed a learned clergy and early Enlightenment. Clan military culture coexists with burgh commerce and North Sea trade.
polities.summary: Presbyterian kingdom in personal union with England until the 1707 parliamentary merger ends separate statehood.
polities.story: The National Covenant (1638) turns a prayer-book quarrel into a constitutional revolution: subjects bind themselves against royal liturgy. Montrose’s royalist campaigns and Cromwell’s victory show Scotland cannot settle its church without English armies. Darien’s collapse and English trade exclusion then push many Lowland elites toward incorporating union—less romance than balance-sheet.
polities.literature: Older makar tradition remembered; ballads and Gaelic song; Sir Thomas Urquhart’s exuberant prose; religious controversy as Scotland’s dominant printed genre; early newspapers and university disputation that will flower into the Scottish Enlightenment after union.
polities.art: Plain kirk interiors reject Catholic images; tower houses and Edinburgh’s vertical Old Town define the built face of the realm; portraiture of Covenanting and Jacobite nobles; Highland dress as identity marker long before romantic tourism.
polities.ideas: George Buchanan’s resistance theory still shadows Stuart kingship; Samuel Rutherford’s Lex, Rex argues law over monarch; Covenanting federal theology shapes political obligation. University Aristotelianism slowly yields to Cartesian and Newtonian curricula by century’s end.

polities.name: Kingdom of Great Britain
polities.description: The 1707 Act of Union creates the Kingdom of Great Britain: one parliament at Westminster, Scots law and Kirk preserved, a shared fiscal-military state. Hanoverian succession (1714) ties the crown to Germany; Walpole’s peace and the Pitts’ wars alternate. By mid-century Britain wins a global duel with France (Seven Years’ War); American independence (1783) wounds but does not end naval and commercial primacy. Mapped 1750–1789 as the island polity facing revolutionary France. Union creates a single parliament at Westminster just as Britain enters the Spanish Succession endgame.
polities.conflicts: Closing phase of the War of the Spanish Succession; War of Jenkins’ Ear / Austrian Succession; Seven Years’ War (annus mirabilis 1759); American Revolutionary War; opening French Revolutionary Wars from 1792. Jacobite threats inland until Culloden (1746).
polities.leaders: Anne; Georges I–III; ministers Walpole, Pelhams, Pitt the Elder, Bute, North, Rockingham, Pitt the Younger. Military names: Marlborough (early), Wolfe, Clive, Rodney, Cornwallis.
polities.religion: Anglican establishment in England and Wales; Presbyterian Scotland; Penal Laws and later relief debates for Catholics; Methodist revival under Wesley reshapes popular piety without disestablishing the church. Toleration remains Protestant-tilted.
polities.culture: Coffee-house and club politics; newspapers and cartoons; a consumer revolution in tea, sugar, cotton; provincial assembly rooms and London season. Empire’s wealth returns as country houses, aquatints of India, and abolitionist agitation by the 1780s.
polities.summary: Hanoverian naval-commercial great power forged by the 1707 union, coalition wars with France, and parliamentary finance.
polities.story: Union sells itself as access to English markets after Darien; within decades the same fiscal state funds global war. Pitt’s annus mirabilis (1759) makes Britain the winner of the mid-century world war; loss of the thirteen colonies then proves that settler assemblies can exit the system. Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations (1776) arrives in the same year as the American Declaration—commerce theorizing itself while empire cracks.
polities.literature: Pope’s couplets and Swift’s satire; Defoe and Richardson invent novelistic realism; Fielding and Sterne play with form; Johnson’s Dictionary and club; Burns’s Scots lyrics; early Romantic signals in Gray and Cowper. Political economy and periodical essays rival poetry as prestige genres.
polities.art: Hogarth’s moral modern moral subjects; Reynolds and the Royal Academy; Gainsborough’s landscapes and society portraits; Canaletto’s London views for Grand Tour taste; Wedgwood’s industrial neoclassical china. Military and naval painting sell victories to a ticket-buying public.
polities.ideas: Scottish and English Enlightenments converge: Hume’s skepticism, Smith’s moral sentiments and markets, Burke’s party and later counter-revolutionary writings, Paine’s radical Rights of Man (1791, just off-tick). Whig constitutionalism becomes a portable ideology of balanced government.

polities.name: Kingdom of Ireland
polities.description: Ireland is a separate kingdom with its own parliament under the English/British crown. Tudor and Stuart conquest, Ulster and other plantations, the 1641 rising, Cromwellian reconquest, and the Williamite War produce a land settlement favoring Protestants. Eighteenth-century Penal Laws structure a Catholic majority under Ascendancy rule; Grattan’s Patriot Parliament asserts legislative dignity within empire. Mapped across all ticks to 1789; the 1798 Rebellion lies just beyond. Flight of the Earls (1607) opens Ulster plantation; 1641’s blood and rumour justify Cromwell’s devastation; the Boyne (1690) decides the Williamite war and seals Penal-era Ascendancy.
polities.conflicts: Nine Years’ War / Tyrone’s rebellion (ending 1603); 1641 rising and Confederate Wars; Cromwellian conquest (1649–53); Williamite War (1689–91) culminating at the Boyne and Limerick; agrarian Whiteboy/Defender violence; 1798 Rebellion just after the 1789 tick.
polities.leaders: Lord Deputies and Lieutenants; Hugh O’Neill (century’s edge); Confederate Catholics; Cromwell as conqueror; James II’s Irish campaign; Williamite commanders; Henry Grattan and Patriot opposition in Dublin.
polities.religion: Church of Ireland as established Protestant church; Catholic majority under Penal restrictions on land, arms, and office; Presbyterian Ulster with its own disabilities and emigration to America. Mass houses, hedge schools, and later relief acts slowly renegotiate confessional hierarchy.
polities.culture: Gaelic bardic decline under plantation; Anglo-Irish estate society and big-house culture; Dublin as a Georgian capital of parliament, theatre, and publishing—often called the second city of the early British world. Folklore, aisling poetry, and harp traditions persist beside English-language Patriot rhetoric.
polities.summary: Kingdom under the English/British crown where plantations, conquest, and Penal Laws entrench a Protestant Ascendancy.
polities.story: The Flight of the Earls (1607) opens Ulster to plantation; 1641’s violence and Cromwell’s response etch sectarian memory for centuries. At the Boyne (1690) a European war over James II is fought on Irish soil and settles Protestant ascendancy. A century later Grattan’s volunteers win legislative independence (1782) without Catholic emancipation—reform without majority inclusion, a fuse for the 1790s.
polities.literature: Gaelic poetry of loss and aisling vision; Anglo-Irish satire and sermon; Swift’s Drapier’s Letters and Modest Proposal as colonial rage in English; Farquhar and later Sheridan from Irish stages; antiquarian collecting of bardic remnants by Ascendancy scholars.
polities.art: Georgian Dublin’s Wide Streets Commissioners and great squares; country-house Palladianism; penal-era Mass houses as vernacular sacred architecture; portraiture of Patriot volunteers; harpers’ gatherings that later feed romantic nationalism.
polities.ideas: Catholic casuistry and continental seminary training (Louvain, Salamanca) sustain a counter-elite; Patriot constitutionalism invokes Molyneux and later American examples; United Irishmen (1790s) will fuse Enlightenment republicanism with confessional grievance just off this map’s edge.

polities.name: Spanish Monarchy
polities.yearsActive: Habsburg composite to 1700; Bourbon Spain thereafter
polities.description: Philip III and IV still rule a European composite—Castile–Aragon, Portugal (to 1640), Italian realms, Franche-Comté, Spanish Netherlands—financed by American silver and asiento debts. Olivares’s Union of Arms strains the system; Catalonia and Portugal revolt (1640). The childless Charles II bequeaths a succession war; Bourbon Philip V keeps the peninsula and empire but surrenders the European outer rings at Utrecht (1713–14). Eighteenth-century ilustrado reform recenters Spain on Madrid and the Atlantic. Olivares tries to make the composite monarchy fight as one machine—and Catalonia and Portugal crack (1640).
polities.conflicts: Eighty Years’ War to 1648; Thirty Years’ War; Franco-Spanish War; Catalan and Portuguese revolts; War of the Spanish Succession; later Italian dynastic wars; Seven Years’ War and American Revolutionary intervention under Charles III.
polities.leaders: Philip III; Philip IV with Olivares; Charles II; Philip V; Ferdinand VI; Charles III; Charles IV. Reform ministers: Ensenada, Floridablanca, Aranda, Campomanes.
polities.religion: Baroque Catholicism: ornate Mass, confraternities, Inquisition still policing belief. Jesuit missions and then expulsion (1767) under Charles III’s regalism. Saints, processions, and imperial mission theology saturate public life even as ilustrados critique scholastic monopoly.
polities.culture: Late Siglo de Oro prestige outlives fiscal decline; Bourbon afrancesado taste then mixes French court models with Spanish urban reform. American silver, cadiz trade, and colonial administration keep Madrid’s eyes on a transatlantic monarchy even after European contraction.
polities.summary: Habsburg composite monarchy that yields to Bourbon Spain after Utrecht, keeping the peninsula and empire but losing European outer rings.
polities.story: Don Quixote (1605/1615) laughs a tired empire into world literature while silver fleets and bankruptcies continue offstage. Rocroi (1643) signals tercios’ fading aura; Utrecht then amputates the European composite. Charles III’s enlightened absolutism—roads, canals, botanical gardens, colonial intendancies—tries to make a modern peninsular-Atlantic state from Habsburg ruins.
polities.literature: Cervantes’s novelistic self-awareness; Lope de Vega and Calderón’s theatrical ocean; Quevedo and Góngora’s dueling styles; María de Zayas; later Feijóo’s Teatro crítico and ilustrado essays that import European science into Spanish prose.
polities.art: Velázquez’s mirror games at court; Zurbarán’s stark saints; Murillo’s soft Seville devotion; Ribera in Naples; later Goya emerging under Charles IV with a darker eye on reason and war. Court dress and armor in portraits keep claiming a world already slipping.
polities.ideas: Scholastic second scholasticism (Suárez) still frames law and international right; arbitristas diagnose decline; Bourbon regalism and Campomanes’s economic societies push utilitarian reform. American debates on indigenous rights echo Las Casas into new colonial codes.

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.description: Portugal appears throughout the ticks as a distinct realm. Dynastic union with Spain (1580–1640) ends in the Restoration War; the House of Braganza rebuilds sovereignty while Dutch and English rivals bite at Asian and Brazilian empires. Brazilian gold and diamonds fund John V’s baroque display; Pombal’s dictatorial reform after the 1755 earthquake recenters the state on enlightened absolutism and British alliance. The 1640 restoration against Spain becomes Portugal’s second independence epic.
polities.conflicts: Dutch–Portuguese colonial wars in Asia, Africa, and Brazil; Restoration War vs Spain (1640–68); Spanish Succession entanglement; Seven Years’ War Iberian campaign (1762); French Revolutionary/Napoleonic crisis ahead. Overseas: struggles over the praças of Morocco and the Indian Ocean.
polities.leaders: Philips of Spain during union; John IV of Braganza; Afonso VI; Peter II; John V; Joseph I with Marquis of Pombal; Maria I. Military restorer António Vieira as preacher-politician of empire.
polities.religion: Catholic kingdom with Inquisition and missionary orders (Jesuits in Brazil and Asia until Pombal’s expulsion, 1759). Pombaline regalism seizes church property and rewrites education as a state project.
polities.culture: Lisbon’s mercantile and courtly culture; Brazilian gold boom aesthetics; azulejo tile narratives; Pombaline grid reconstruction as a modern urban ideology after 1755. Alliance with Britain shapes elite taste and trade (Methuen Treaty’s wine-for-cloth pattern).
polities.summary: Braganza Atlantic kingdom restored from Spanish union, rebuilt on Brazilian gold and Pombaline reform after 1755.
polities.story: The 1640 restoration against Spain becomes Portugal’s second independence epic, preached by Vieira as providential empire. A century later the All Saints’ Day earthquake levels Lisbon; Pombal rebuilds the Baixa on rational streets and breaks Jesuit power—catastrophe as a lever for absolutist modernity.
polities.literature: Camões still the national epic touchstone; Vieira’s sermons as baroque politics; Ribeiro Sanches and foreign-letter literati; later arcádia neoclassical poetry. Travel and colonial reportage form a parallel literature of factories and captaincies.
polities.art: Joanine baroque and the Convent of Mafra as gold-fueled sacral display; azulejos narrating battles and saints; Pombaline neoclassical façades; Brazilian colonial baroque as the empire’s other face. Court portraiture tracks Braganza legitimacy after union.
polities.ideas: Sebastianist messianism and Vieira’s fifth-empire theology haunt politics; estrangeirados import French and English reform ideas; Pombal’s utilitarian statecraft privileges useful knowledge over scholastic colleges.

polities.name: Lower Navarre
polities.yearsActive: French Navarre rump to early Bourbon absorption
polities.description: Lower Navarre north of the Pyrenees remains the last distinct Navarrese outline tied to Henry IV’s patrimony, shown at the 1600 tick before full administrative merger into France. It is a Basque-Romance border society under the French crown rather than a field-power kingdom—symbolic of how early modern composites absorb medieval dynastic remnants. The kingdom that gave France a Bourbon king disappears as a map colour—Henry IV’s patrimonial Navarre is the seed of a dynasty that will rule from Paris, not Pau.
polities.conflicts: No major independent campaigns in this era; security follows French Wars of Religion settlements and later Franco-Spanish Pyrenean diplomacy (Treaty of the Pyrenees, 1659, nearby).
polities.leaders: Henry IV as King of France and Navarre; Louis XIII during administrative absorption.
polities.religion: Catholic after the Wars of Religion settlement; memory of Jeanne d’Albret’s Calvinist court still colors local Protestant pockets before broader French confessional pressure.
polities.culture: Basque and Gascon speech worlds; Pyrenean pastoral and border-market habits; loyalty rituals to a king who is more Parisian than Pamplonan.
polities.summary: Tiny French Navarre rump—Henry IV’s patrimony—mapped at 1600 before full Bourbon absorption.
polities.story: When Henry of Navarre becomes Henry IV of France, his little Pyrenean realm hitchhikes into Bourbon history—then disappears as a separate outline while the royal title ‘King of France and Navarre’ lingers on coins and proclamations like a fossil.
polities.literature: Local fueros and customary law texts matter more than court poetry; French royal ordinances gradually overwrite Navarrese distinctiveness in administrative prose.
polities.art: Modest court residue at Pau; vernacular church art of the western Pyrenees; no Versailles-scale patronage—this is a border remnant, not a cultural capital.
polities.ideas: Foral legal particularism—the idea that custom binds the prince—survives as a local political instinct even as Gallican absolutism centralizes from Paris.

polities.name: Dutch Republic (United Provinces)
polities.description: The United Provinces fight Spain to Westphalian recognition (1648), then punch above their weight as a naval, colonial, and financial hub. Stadtholders of Orange alternate with True Freedom republican regimes (de Witt). Anglo-Dutch and Franco-Dutch wars erode primacy, yet the Republic remains independent at 1789 before the Batavian Revolution. Federal towns, not a court capital, drive politics. A revolt against Spain becomes the richest experiment in federal commerce.
polities.conflicts: Eighty Years’ War; Anglo-Dutch Wars (three in the 17th c., a fourth 1780–84); Franco-Dutch War (1672, the Disaster Year); Nine Years’ War and War of the Spanish Succession as William III’s coalition partner; internal Patriot vs Orangist strife in the 1780s.
polities.leaders: Maurice and Frederick Henry of Nassau; Johan and Cornelis de Witt; William III (also king of England); later Orange stadtholders. Admirals Tromp and De Ruyter as republican heroes.
polities.religion: Public Reformed (Calvinist) church with remarkable urban pluralism: Catholics, Lutherans, Jews, and dissenting sects trade and worship under varying tolerances—Arminian controversies (Synod of Dort, 1618–19) cut deep.
polities.culture: Canal-city burgher culture; VOC and WIC global companies; stock exchange and public debt techniques; print, cartography, and news as exports. Cleanliness, Calvinist sobriety, and luxury still-life paradoxically coexist in the same parlors.
polities.summary: Federal Calvinist commercial republic whose Golden Age finance and art peak before Anglo-French pressure.
polities.story: 1672—the Disaster Year—sees France and England pile on; the orphaned Republic nearly drowns until De Ruyter’s seamanship and William III’s rise stabilize it. A century earlier, the Twelve Years’ Truce and Westphalia had certified that a merchant federation could beat a world monarchy. Spinoza’s lens-grinding exile philosophy is the quiet twin of that political experiment.
polities.literature: Vondel’s tragedies; Cats’s didactic bestsellers; Huygens’s courtly verse; travel and company reports; a dense pamphlet sphere. Multilingual Amsterdam publishes what other censors refuse.
polities.art: Rembrandt’s light theology; Vermeer’s domestic optics; Hals’s civic militia bravura; Ruisdael’s skies; still life as moral inventory. The art market—not a single prince—is the patron, and that shows in genre scale and subject.
polities.ideas: Grotius’s natural law and free seas; Arminian vs Gomarist theology as political fault line; Spinoza’s Tractatus and Ethics as radical Enlightenment from inside the Republic; Bayle publishing in Rotterdam. Republican True Freedom ideology vs Orange monarchical leanings.

polities.name: Spanish Netherlands
polities.description: After the Dutch Revolt splits the Low Countries, the southern provinces remain under Spanish Habsburg sovereignty: a fortified corridor of towns from Flanders to Luxembourg. Archdukes Albert and Isabella give a courtly Catholic restoration; later governors defend against French advance. At Utrecht/Rastatt (1713–14) the territory passes to the Austrian Habsburgs—ending the Spanish Netherlands layer on this map. The south stays Spanish and Catholic when the north peels away.
polities.conflicts: Closing Eighty Years’ War; Franco-Dutch War; Reunion wars of Louis XIV; Nine Years’ War; War of the Spanish Succession with sieges across Flanders and Brabant. Barrier fortresses become European bargaining chips.
polities.leaders: Archdukes Albert and Isabella; governors under Philip IV and Charles II (including Don Juan of Austria the Younger); military intendants facing Luxembourg and Vauban’s French frontier system.
polities.religion: Tridentine Catholicism restored after revolt; Jesuits and Capuchins rebuild urban piety; Protestant remnant emigrates or goes quiet. Marian and Corpus Christi processions reclaim public space.
polities.culture: Brussels court culture under the archdukes; Antwerp’s publishing and art recovery; French linguistic pressure in elite circles beside Dutch dialects. A borderland learning to live as Europe’s cockpit.
polities.summary: Catholic southern Low Countries—Habsburg buffer repeatedly fought over until Utrecht hands them to Austria.
polities.story: Rubens paints diplomacy as much as altarpieces—court painter, knight, and negotiator between courts. Louis XIV’s advances turn Flanders into a geometry of sieges; by Utrecht the Spanish crown trades these provinces away, ending a century of Catholic Habsburg holding action.
polities.literature: Counter-Reformation sermon and emblem books; vernacular drama in Antwerp and Brussels; multilingual administrative prose. Print culture remains dense even as political primacy fades.
polities.art: Rubens’s muscular baroque altarpieces and Whitehall ceiling diplomacy; Van Dyck emerging from his studio; Jordaens’s abundant Flemish bodies; tapestry workshops still exporting grandeur. Church interiors become theatres of Catholic triumph.
polities.ideas: Justus Lipsius’s neo-Stoicism from Leuven influences European statecraft; Counter-Reformation casuistry and Jesuit education shape elites; legal defense of Habsburg sovereignty against French claims.

polities.name: Austrian Netherlands
polities.description: Awarded to Austria after the War of the Spanish Succession, the southern Low Countries are governed from Brussels with local estates guarding privileges. Maria Theresa’s regime is relatively light; Joseph II’s reforming blizzard—seminaries, language, guilds, liturgy—triggers the Brabant Revolution (1789–90). Mapped 1750–1789 as a Habsburg possession on France’s northern doorstep. Utrecht makes these provinces Austrian.
polities.conflicts: War of the Austrian Succession (French occupation episodes); diplomatic revolutions of the mid-century; Brabant Revolution (1789–90) against Josephist centralisation.
polities.leaders: Charles VI; Maria Theresa; Joseph II; governors-general in Brussels (Charles of Lorraine notable). Local estate leaders and Vonckist/Statist factions in 1789.
polities.religion: Deep Catholic society; Joseph II’s Patent reforms, seminary control, and liturgical interference provoke clerical and popular resistance more fierce than in many German lands.
polities.culture: Late baroque and rococo Brussels and Antwerp; French as elite language; thriving lace, coal, and textile regions. Estates particularism as a political culture of privilege.
polities.summary: Former Spanish Netherlands under Vienna—prosperous, Catholic, and restive under Joseph II.
polities.story: Joseph II tries to make the Netherlands as uniform as Austria’s other experiments; instead he teaches local elites how to revolt in the name of old constitutions. The Brabant Revolution briefly invents the United Belgian States—an early modern privilege revolt wearing Enlightenment colors—just as France’s own revolution ignites next door.
polities.literature: Legal remonstrances and estate pamphlets as the era’s vital genre; French-language journalism; devotional and antiquarian writing claiming medieval privileges as living law.
polities.art: Rococo church refurbishments; courtly decoration under Charles of Lorraine; civic portraiture of estate leaders; urban festive culture that doubles as political display.
polities.ideas: Statist constitutionalism vs Vonckist more open reformism—both claim Enlightenment vocabulary while defending or revising provincial charters. Physiocratic and cameralist imports filter through Brussels administration.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.description: The Holy Roman Empire remains a mosaic of electorates, duchies, free cities, prince-bishoprics, and imperial knights. The Thirty Years’ War and Peace of Westphalia (1648) confirm territorial sovereignty (Landeshoheit) for estates and recognize Dutch and Swiss exits. Emperors from the Habsburg line still matter, but great-power politics increasingly runs through Vienna and Berlin. Still the legal frame of Central Europe in 1789. Defenestration (1618) to Westphalia (1648): a generation of war hollows German lands.
polities.conflicts: Thirty Years’ War as defining catastrophe; Franco-imperial wars under Louis XIV; War of the Austrian Succession; Seven Years’ War as both great-power and quasi-civil war; Bavarian Succession. Perpetual Diet at Regensburg institutionalizes negotiation over annihilation.
polities.leaders: Rudolf II (edge); Ferdinand II/III; Leopold I; Joseph I; Charles VI; Charles VII (Wittelsbach interlude); Francis I; Joseph II; Leopold II from 1790. Imperial estates and electors as co-sovereigns.
polities.religion: Augsburg and Westphalia’s cuius regio / normative year rules freeze a map of Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed territories; imperial courts adjudicate confessional lawsuits. Pietism and later Catholic Enlightenment soften pastoral practice inside the legal shell.
polities.culture: Princely Residenz cities multiply courts and opera houses; imperial free cities guard burgher liberties; university towns (Halle, Göttingen, Jena) invent the modern research seminar. Baroque pilgrimage churches dot Catholic landscapes; Bach’s Saxony shows Lutheran music at its height.
polities.summary: Decentralized imperial legal frame of Central Europe after Westphalia—still real in 1789, driven by Austria and Prussia.
polities.story: Westphalia ends the fantasy of confessional reconquest and turns the Empire into a legal peace system—messy, multilayered, and surprisingly durable. When Frederick II seizes Silesia, the imperial constitution cannot stop him; it can only process the shock through diets, guarantees, and new alliances. The Reich’s weakness is also its pacifying strength.
polities.literature: Gruebelnde baroque poetry and Opitz’s reforms; Grimmelshausen’s Simplicissimus as war’s memory; later Klopstock, Lessing’s public criticism, and the early Sturm und Drang. Latin remains a scholarly lingua franca beside emerging Hochdeutsch.
polities.art: South German and Austrian baroque churches (Asam, Neumann’s residences); Dresden’s court splendors; Protestant musical architecture of Bach and Handel (Handel exported); porcelain (Meissen) as white gold. Dress codes broadcast estate rank in a society without a single capital.
polities.ideas: Reichspublizistik—constitutional writing about the Empire itself—becomes a science of mixed government (Pufendorf, later Moser). Natural law from Leipzig and Halle; Wolffian rationalism; Kant at Königsberg on the Empire’s northeastern edge by late century. Cameralism trains officials for tiny states.

polities.name: Habsburg Monarchy (Austria)
polities.description: The Habsburg Monarchy is a dynastic conglomerate: Alpine hereditary lands, Bohemian crown after White Mountain, reconquest of Hungary from the Ottomans (1683–99), then Austrian Netherlands and Milan after Utrecht, and Galicia from the First Partition of Poland (1772). It is Vienna-centered, multiethnic, and locked in rivalry first with the Porte, then with Prussia. Maria Theresa and Joseph II redefine statehood without becoming a nation-state. Sobieski’s relief of Vienna (1683) opens the Habsburg reconquest of Hungary.
polities.conflicts: Long Turkish War aftermath; Great Turkish War (Vienna 1683 to Karlowitz 1699); War of the Spanish Succession; Austrian Succession (Silesia lost); Seven Years’ War; War of the Bavarian Succession; Ottoman wars under Maria Theresa/Joseph II.
polities.leaders: Ferdinand II/III; Leopold I; Joseph I; Charles VI; Maria Theresa; Joseph II; co-ministers Kaunitz, Eugene of Savoy as military architect of the reconquest.
polities.religion: Catholic dynasty driving Contre-Reformation in Bohemia and Hungary; later Josephist toleration patents (1781) for Protestants and Jews reshape confessional law. Uniate and Orthodox populations on the eastern edges complicate uniformity.
polities.culture: Vienna as imperial-musical capital—court opera, later classical style; Hungarian and Bohemian estates inside one dynastic system; Italian and Netherlandish provinces after 1714. Multiethnic kitchens, uniforms, and bureaucracies invent a composite loyalty.
polities.summary: Danubian Habsburg composite that reconquers Hungary, gains Italian and Netherlandish lands, and partitions Poland.
polities.story: Sobieski’s relief of Vienna (1683) and Eugene’s victories turn Ottoman tide; Karlowitz (1699) remakes the Hungarian plain as Habsburg. The Pragmatic Sanction’s gamble nearly fails when Frederick II steals Silesia—Maria Theresa’s survival myth becomes the monarchy’s founding modern story. Joseph II then tries to rationalize what dynasty had only accumulated.
polities.literature: Court Italian opera libretti; German occasional verse; Hungarian and Czech estate petitions; later Sonnenfels’s Enlightenment journalism in Vienna. Administrative German slowly becomes a supraregional prose.
polities.art: Fischer von Erlach and Hildebrandt’s baroque Vienna; Belvedere for Eugene; Bohemian and Alpine pilgrimage architecture; court theatrical design. Uniforms and equestrian portraits sell dynastic continuity across languages.
polities.ideas: Cameralism and police sciences in Vienna; Kaunitz’s diplomatic revolution (alliance with France); Josephinism as utilitarian Christian reform; natural-law justifications for the Pragmatic Sanction and later toleration.

polities.name: Brandenburg–Prussia / Kingdom of Prussia
polities.description: Brandenburg–Prussia unites Rhineland scraps, Berlin’s electorate, and Ducal Prussia; Westphalia adds Eastern Pomerania pieces; the royal title in Prussia (1701) elevates the dynasty. Frederick William I builds the canton army and thrift; Frederick II seizes Silesia (1740s) and survives the Seven Years’ War. First Partition (1772) adds West Prussia, linking cores. By 1789 a bureaucratic-military great power. From battered electorate to drill kingdom: the Great Elector builds an army the state exists to feed.
polities.conflicts: Thirty Years’ War occupation and aftermath; Swedish-Polish wars; Great Northern War orbit; Silesian Wars / Austrian Succession; Seven Years’ War (survival against coalition); First Partition of Poland (1772) with territorial gains.
polities.leaders: John Sigismund; Great Elector Frederick William; Frederick I (king in Prussia); Frederick William I; Frederick II (the Great); Frederick William II. Ministers and generals: Hertzberg, Seydlitz, Zieten.
polities.religion: Calvinist rulers over mostly Lutheran subjects—an unusual Hohenzollern arrangement—with pragmatic toleration for useful immigrants (Huguenots after 1685). Pietism shapes education and officer ethos more than baroque Catholicism does.
polities.culture: Spartan court under the Soldier King; Francophone Sanssouci culture under Frederick II; canton system and beamten bureaucracy as social forms; Pietist Halle influencing schooling and obedience.
polities.summary: Hohenzollern militarized state—from Brandenburg electorate to great power via Silesia and partition.
polities.story: Frederick II’s seizure of Silesia (1740) is a crime that founds great-power Prussia—then the Seven Years’ War nearly erases it until Russian exit (1762) saves Berlin’s king. Partition diplomacy later grows the realm without a Frederickean miracle, binding Prussia to the Polish question.
polities.literature: Frederick’s own French writings; early Berlin Enlightenment journals; Lessing’s ties to Prussian stages; soldier songs and administrative prose as the realm’s true vernacular genres.
polities.art: Knobelsdorff’s Sanssouci rococo; Berlin opera; Antoine Pesne portraits; later stricter neoclassical tastes. Uniform blue and the Mitre cap become visual trademarks more famous than painting schools.
polities.ideas: Cameralist duty-state; Frederick’s enlightened absolutism—philosopher-king rhetoric with censorship still real; religious toleration as raison d’état; anti-Machiavel posing beside Realpolitik.

polities.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polities.description: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth is a vast elective monarchy of noble democracy (sejm, liberum veto) spanning Catholic, Orthodox, Uniate, Lutheran, and Jewish communities. Seventeenth-century wars with Sweden, Muscovy, and Cossack revolt (Khmelnytsky) wreck the core; eighteenth-century Russian influence turns reform into crisis. First Partition (1772) truncates the map; by 1789 the Commonwealth still exists, racing reform against further partition. Sobieski saves Vienna (1683) at the Commonwealth’s military dusk.
polities.conflicts: Polish–Swedish wars; Khmelnytsky Uprising; Russo-Polish wars; Swedish Deluge (1655–60); Great Northern War theatres; War of the Polish Succession; Bar Confederation; First Partition (1772). Ottoman wars including Chocim/Khotyn and Vienna relief under Sobieski.
polities.leaders: Sigismund III Vasa; Władysław IV; John II Casimir; Michael Korybut; John III Sobieski; Augustus II/III (Wettins); Stanisław August Poniatowski. Magnate factions as co-rulers in practice.
polities.religion: Catholic dominance after earlier Warsaw Confederation tolerance frays; Union of Brest creates Uniate church; Orthodox, Protestant, and large Jewish communities under varying protections. Confessional politics intertwine with Russian and Habsburg intervention.
polities.culture: Sarmatian noble culture—kontusz dress, Latin-Polish bilingualism, estate hospitality; Jewish shtetl and kahal autonomy; Cossack borderlands. Warsaw and Wilno as political-cultural poles of a dual commonwealth.
polities.summary: Elective noble republic whose Golden Liberty ends in the Partitions after seventeenth-century wars.
polities.story: Sobieski’s charge at Vienna (1683) is the Commonwealth’s last European heroics abroad while the Deluge’s memory still scars home. A century later Stanisław August’s enlightened court and the Commission of National Education try to reform a veto-bound republic; the First Partition shows neighbors will carve what diets cannot defend.
polities.literature: Baroque Sarmatian panegyric; Kochowski’s war verse; later Krasicki’s fables and satires under Stanisław August; political writing of the Four-Year Sejm brewing off the late tick. Hebrew and Yiddish letters thrive in parallel urban worlds.
polities.art: Wilhelms and later Saxon-Wettin court tastes in Warsaw; sacred baroque of Catholic and Uniate churches; manor portraiture of magnates; kontusz sash and karabela sabre as wearable ideology.
polities.ideas: Golden Liberty as anti-absolutist ideology—attractive and self-paralyzing; reform thought of Konarski and later collégial education; physiocratic and constitutional drafts under Poniatowski; debates on cities’ and Jews’ civic status.

polities.name: Swedish Empire / Kingdom of Sweden
polities.yearsActive: Baltic great-power age c. 1611–1721; kingdom continues
polities.description: Sweden builds a military allotment empire across the Baltic: Finland, Estonia, Livonia, western Pomerania, Bremen-Verden, and briefly Danish Scanian lands. Gustavus Adolphus intervenes in the Thirty Years’ War; Charles X and XI consolidate; Charles XII’s Great Northern War (against Russia, Saxony-Poland, Denmark) ends in imperial overstretch and Nystad (1721) losses. Eighteenth-century Sweden becomes a reduced kingdom with Age of Liberty politics then Gustavian recentralization. Gustavus Adolphus lands in Germany (1630) and dies at Lützen—a Protestant lion whose reforms outlive him.
polities.conflicts: Ingrian and Polish wars; Thirty Years’ War; Northern Wars vs Denmark-Norway; Scanian War; Great Northern War; Hats’ and Caps’ wars with Russia; later Gustavian Russian war (1788–90).
polities.leaders: Charles IX; Gustavus Adolphus; Christina; Charles X Gustav; Charles XI; Charles XII; Ulrika Eleonora; Frederick I; Adolph Frederick; Gustav III.
polities.religion: Lutheran confessional state (Uppsala 1593 legacy) with tight clerical control; Pietist currents later; Catholic and Calvinist minorities marginal under uniformity laws.
polities.culture: Allotment (indelningsverk) society militarizes the countryside; Baltic administrative culture in German and Swedish; Gustavian neoclassicism and court theatre in Stockholm after mid-century.
polities.summary: Baltic imperial stormakt that crashes in the Great Northern War and reinvents itself as a lesser scientific kingdom.
polities.story: Gustavus Adolphus lands in Germany (1630) and dies at Lützen—a Protestant lion whose reforms outlive him. Charles XII rides the empire to Poltava (1709) and breaks it. Nystad (1721) hands the eastern Baltic to Russia; Sweden reinvents itself as a constitutional and scientific kingdom on a smaller map.
polities.literature: Stiernhielm as ‘father of Swedish poetry’; baroque occasional verse; later Bellman songs in Stockholm; Gustavian drama. War diaries and officers’ letters form a parallel epic of the Baltic empire.
polities.art: Tessin’s baroque Stockholm; Karlskrona naval city as planned military art; later Sergel sculpture and Gustavian furniture neoclassicism. Uniforms and captured trophies furnish a visual memory of empire.
polities.ideas: Cameralist and Lutheran household discipline; Age of Liberty party ideology (Hats/Caps); Gustav III’s enlightened despotism with French cultural imports; early freedom of the press experiments (1766 ordinance) unique in Europe for a time.

polities.name: Denmark–Norway
polities.description: Denmark–Norway holds the Sound and, until Roskilde (1658), Scania and other southern Swedish provinces. Christian IV’s ambitions collide with Sweden’s rise; Frederick III’s 1660 absolutist coup remakes the constitution after battlefield humiliation. Thereafter a secondary Baltic power with Norwegian resources, Atlantic trade, and Schleswig-Holstein dynastic knots—still dual at 1789. Christian IV’s ambitions smash against Sweden and the Thirty Years’ War.
polities.conflicts: Kalmar War; Torstenson War; Danish-Swedish wars culminating at Roskilde; Scanian War; Great Northern War; later armed neutrality experiments. Colonial footholds in India, Caribbean, and West Africa as side theatres.
polities.leaders: Christian IV; Frederick III (absolutism 1660); Christian V; Frederick IV; later Oldenburg kings including Christian VII’s troubled reign and Struensee’s brief reform dictatorship (1770–72).
polities.religion: Lutheran state church on the German-Scandinavian model; Pietist reform currents; tight control of dissent in a confessional absolute monarchy.
polities.culture: Copenhagen absolutist court; Norwegian timber, fish, and later shipping periphery; Sound Toll as fiscal worldview; Holberg’s Dano-Norwegian letters binding the dual realm in satire.
polities.summary: Oldenburg dual monarchy that loses Baltic primacy to Sweden and consolidates absolutism after 1660.
polities.story: Roskilde (1658) amputates the Scanian provinces and ends Danish claims to Baltic hegemony; absolute monarchy is the domestic answer to that trauma. A century later Struensee’s Enlightenment decrees—press freedom, reform—flash and fall, showing how thin absolutist modernization can be without elite buy-in.
polities.literature: Ludvig Holberg’s comedies and essays as the North’s Enlightenment voice; king’s laws and hymnals; Norwegian topographical writings; later lyric beginnings toward a dual-kingdom public.
polities.art: Dutch-influenced Copenhagen painting; absolute monarchy’s castles (Rosenborg earlier, later Fredensborg); naval imagery; Norwegian stave-church survival beside Lutheran whitewashed interiors.
polities.ideas: Lutheran household patriarchalism; Lex Regia (1665) as one of Europe’s starkest absolutist charters; Struensee’s imported Enlightenment utilitarianism; cameralist management of Norway as resource colony.

polities.name: Tsardom / Russian Empire
polities.description: Recovery after the Time of Troubles brings the Romanovs; Alexis consolidates; Peter I drags the realm toward European military and naval forms, founding St Petersburg (1703) and winning Baltic provinces at Nystad (1721). Elizabeth and Catherine II expand against Ottomans and the Commonwealth; Crimea is annexed (1783); partitions add Lithuanian-Belarusian-Ukrainian lands. By 1789 a Eurasian empire anchors eastern Europe. Peter forces a window on the Baltic—Poltava (1709) and Nystad (1721) announce a new great power.
polities.conflicts: Polish–Muscovite wars; Russo-Swedish wars; Thirteen Years’ War; Great Northern War; Russo-Turkish wars (especially 1768–74, 1787–92); participation in Polish partitions; Pugachev Rebellion as internal war.
polities.leaders: Boris Godunov (edge); Michael and Alexis Romanov; Sophia’s regency; Peter I; Anna; Elizabeth; Peter III; Catherine II. Favorites and reformers: Menshikov, Potemkin, Panin.
polities.religion: Russian Orthodox Church as state sacral frame; Nikonian reforms and Old Believer schism (Raskol); Peter’s synodal control subordinating the patriarchate; Catherine’s selective toleration and Muslim policies in annexed lands.
polities.culture: Muscovite ritual court yields to Petrine beard-tax modernity and Catherinian Francophone aristocracy; serfdom hardens even as capitals Europeanize. Ukrainian, Baltic German, and Tatar worlds are governed inside one imperial repertoire of uniforms and ranks (Table of Ranks).
polities.summary: Romanov empire that opens a Baltic window under Peter and expands under Catherine to Crimea and partitioned Poland.
polities.story: Peter’s victory at Poltava (1709) relocates Russia into European great-power politics; St Petersburg is the stone metaphor of that turn. Catherine’s Nakaz and Legislative Commission flirt with Enlightenment law while Pugachev’s revolt (1773–75) reminds the empire that serfdom is its furnace—and its fire hazard.
polities.literature: Sermons and chronographs; Simeon Polotsky’s baroque court verse; later Sumarokov and Lomonosov invent modern Russian literary language; Derzhavin’s odes; Radishchev’s Journey (1790) just off-tick as autocratic Enlightenment’s guilty conscience.
polities.art: Icon tradition under pressure from Western portraiture; Petrine engraving and fortress cities; Rastrelli’s baroque palaces; early neoclassicism under Catherine; parade uniforms as wearable art of rank.
polities.ideas: Third Rome religious-political residue; Peter’s forced Westernization; Feofan Prokopovich’s absolutist theology; Catherine’s corresponding with Voltaire/Diderot while consolidating autocracy; official nationality still unformed but Orthodoxy–autocracy–empire already practiced.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire (European lands)
polities.description: At 1600–1648 the Porte still holds the central Hungarian corridor, Balkans, and Greek lands. The Great Turkish War and Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) surrender most of Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs; Passarowitz and later Russo-Turkish wars trim further edges. Provincial ayans rise as Istanbul’s grip loosens, yet Rumelia and the Aegean core remain Ottoman at 1789. Europe meets the empire as threat, trade partner, and orientalist fantasy. Kara Mustafa’s failed siege of Vienna (1683) opens a long retreat from the Danube middle.
polities.conflicts: Long Turkish War aftermath; Cretan War vs Venice; Great Turkish War (1683–99); wars with Habsburgs, Venice, Poland, and Russia; Hotin/Khotyn and Pruth campaigns; late-century wars with Catherine II.
polities.leaders: Mehmed III; Ahmed I; Murad IV; Mehmed IV; Köprülü viziers; later 18th-c. sultans including Ahmed III (Tulip Era) and Selim III just at the edge of reform. Crimean Giray khans as vassal sword-arm.
polities.religion: Sunni Islamic empire with ulema and sultan-caliph prestige; millet administration for Orthodox, Armenian, and Jewish communities; Sufi orders in urban life; Muslim elites layered over Balkan Christians.
polities.culture: Topkapı court culture, then later shoreline palaces; coffeehouse and tulip aesthetics; provincial ayan households; Greek Phanariot administrators linking Orthodoxy to Ottoman governance. Devshirme fades as timar systems mutate.
polities.summary: Still-European empire of Rumelia that retreats from Hungary after 1683 yet holds the Balkans into 1789.
polities.story: The failure before Vienna (1683) and Karlowitz’s map rewrite end the age when European diplomacy assumed Ottoman strategic offense in the Danube basin. The Tulip Era (early 1700s) briefly stages consumption and pleasure in Istanbul while military reform debates simmer—an empire learning to live as one great power among others, not the scourge of Christendom alone.
polities.literature: Divan poetry still prestigious; Evliya Çelebi’s Seyahatname as vast travel prose; chronicles of court and campaign; Greek, Armenian, and Slavic Christian literatures under millet skies; diplomatic translations as a growing genre.
polities.art: Classical Ottoman mosque architecture’s afterglow; tile revetments; miniature painting yielding partly to Europeanizing portrait experiments; Tulip Era leisure imagery; Balkan Orthodox church art continuing under Islamic sovereignty.
polities.ideas: Hanafi legal continuity; advice literature (nasihatname) diagnosing decline; early interest in European military technique; Kâtip Çelebi’s geographic and bibliographic encyclopedism; debates on innovation (bid‘a) vs necessary reform.

polities.name: Royal Hungary
polities.description: Mapped at 1600–1648 as the Habsburg-controlled strip of the medieval Hungarian crown, pressed between Ottoman Hungary and Transylvania. Magnates, palatines, and frontier captains run a fortress society. After Karlowitz the reconquered plain is administered within the Habsburg Monarchy layer rather than as a separate outline. Royal Hungary is a rump kingdom living in forts—Ender of Ottoman and Transylvanian pressure.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman frontier wars and castle sieges; Fifteen Years’ War echoes; anti-Habsburg noble conspiracies; Rákóczi War of Independence (1703–11) just after the separate Hungary layer ends.
polities.leaders: Habsburg kings Ferdinand II/III and successors as apostolic kings; Hungarian palatines and estate diet leaders; frontier captains of the Military Border forming nearby.
polities.religion: Catholic Habsburg restoration pressure vs strong Protestant (especially Calvinist) noble networks; Orthodox populations in the south; later Uniate projects. Confession follows castle loyalties.
polities.culture: Magyar noble estate politics; Latin of the diet; hajdú and frontier military folklore; wine and cattle economies feeding Vienna and Italy. A kingdom remembered as crown even when territory is a crescent.
polities.summary: Royal Hungary—Habsburg northern/western remnant on the Ottoman frontier until reconquest folds it into Vienna’s monarchy.
polities.story: While Buda still sits under Ottoman rule, Pressburg/Pozsony hosts Habsburg coronations—Hungary as legal fiction and fortress reality at once. Reconquest after 1683 returns the plain but imports Military Frontier colonization and Vienna’s control, setting up Rákóczi’s early-eighteenth-century revolt.
polities.literature: Latin diet oratory; Hungarian Protestant preaching and psalm culture; epic memory of Mohács; camp letters from the frontier. Print is thinner than in the German lands but politically sharp.
polities.art: Castle architecture and palisade forts; Catholic baroque arriving with Jesuits; Protestant plain churches; coronation regalia as portable kingdom. Ottoman-era Buda leaves baths and ruined palaces.
polities.ideas: Holy Crown doctrine—the kingdom as a legal person beyond the king; estate resistance rights; Protestant constitutionalism against Vienna’s Contre-Reformation absolutism.

polities.name: Principality of Transylvania
polities.description: Transylvania navigates between Vienna and Istanbul as a semi-independent principality with a recognized multi-confessional estate system. Princes like Gábor Bethlen intervene in the Thirty Years’ War against Habsburgs. After the Great Turkish War, Habsburg incorporation ends separate mapping (post-1648 in this pack). Bethlen Gábor plays the Thirty Years’ War like a chessboard, raiding Habsburg Hungary while paying Ottoman tribute.
polities.conflicts: Anti-Habsburg campaigns of Bocskai, Bethlen, and the Rákóczis; Ottoman–Habsburg wars fought across its diplomacy; internal estate strife among Magyar, Székely, Saxon, and Romanian worlds.
polities.leaders: Stephen Bocskai; Gábor Bethlen; György Rákóczi I and II; Mihály Apafi. Diet of estates as continuous co-ruler.
polities.religion: Legal recognition for Catholic, Reformed, Lutheran, and Unitarian estates—rare early modern pluralism; Orthodox Romanians numerous yet politically disadvantaged. A laboratory of negotiated confessions.
polities.culture: Magyar Reformed elite culture; Saxon towns with German law; Romanian village worlds; Ottoman tribute diplomacy as everyday statecraft. Alba Iulia/Gyulafehérvár as princely stage.
polities.summary: Ottoman-suzerain principality—Protestant power-broker of the Carpathians in the Thirty Years’ War era.
polities.story: Bethlen’s wars and diplomacy show how a Carpathian principality can tip German confessional conflict while paying tribute to the sultan. The same balancing act becomes impossible once Habsburgs take Hungary’s plain—Transylvania’s autonomy is the first casualty of Ottoman retreat.
polities.literature: Reformed school drama and catechisms; Saxon municipal chronicles; princely propaganda in Latin and Hungarian; Unitarian theological polemics unique in Europe for their public estate status.
polities.art: Fortified Saxon churches; princely palaces at Alba Iulia; plain Reformed interiors vs Catholic restoration attempts; costume of the four (or more) nations as political fashion.
polities.ideas: Estate constitutionalism with explicit confessional pluralism; anti-Habsburg ‘liberties’ ideology; Unitarian theology as a lived political option, not merely a heresy hunted.

polities.name: Lands of the Bohemian Crown
polities.description: Bohemia, Moravia, and Silesia enter the era as Habsburg-ruled lands with strong Protestant estates. The 1618 Defenestration ignites the Thirty Years’ War; White Mountain (1620) breaks the revolt and triggers confiscations, exile, and forced re-Catholicization. The Bohemian layer on this map runs through 1700; Silesia’s later seizure by Prussia is carried on the Prussia/Austria layers. Two governors fly from a Prague window (1618); Europe catches fire.
polities.conflicts: Bohemian Revolt (1618–20); Thirty Years’ War campaigns across the crown lands; later Silesian Wars under Maria Theresa that peel Silesia away after this layer ends.
polities.leaders: Frederick V (Winter King); Ferdinand II; Wallenstein as war entrepreneur in Bohemian lands; later Habsburg sovereigns ruling through gubernia.
polities.religion: Forced re-Catholicization after 1620; Jesuit colleges; Protestant exile to Saxony and beyond; folk Catholicism fused with baroque pilgrimage. Czech Utraquist memory goes underground.
polities.culture: Czech vernacular pressed by Germanizing elites; baroque rebuilding of Prague; serfdom tightened on estates granted to loyalists. A crown land inside the Habsburg composite, not an independent actor.
polities.summary: Crown lands whose 1618 revolt ignites the Thirty Years’ War and whose defeat brings forced re-Catholicization.
polities.story: Defenestration (1618) makes Prague the spark of a German-European war; White Mountain two years later ends estate dualism for a century. Comenius carries Bohemian Protestant pedagogy into European exile—the kingdom’s ideas leave when its nobles cannot stay.
polities.literature: Comenius’s didactic and pansophic Latin works; Czech hymn and exile writing; German baroque sermons in reconverted pulpits; later Czech revival seeds still dormant under official German.
polities.art: Prague’s baroque remaking—St Nicholas, Charles Bridge statues; aristocratic palaces on confiscated ground; rural pilgrimage churches. Gothic Charles University’s city becomes a Catholic stage set.
polities.ideas: Estate constitutionalism crushed then mourned; Comenius’s pansophia and universal education; Jesuit scholasticism as the new official mind; early German cameralism in provincial administration.

polities.name: Swiss Confederation
polities.yearsActive: De facto independence long before; recognized 1648
polities.description: The Swiss Confederation remains a patchwork of sovereign cantons and associates, Catholic and Reformed. Westphalia (1648) recognizes independence from the Empire. Internal confessional wars (Villmergen) flare, but the diet (Tagsatzung) generally keeps the league out of great-power partitions. Mercenary contracts and alpine transit taxes fund particularism into 1789. The Confederation exits the Empire on paper in 1648, confirming what arms and diplomacy already made real.
polities.conflicts: First and Second Villmergen Wars; occasional French and imperial pressure; generally avoids direct great-power wars while exporting soldiers to them.
polities.leaders: Cantonal councils; Tagsatzung diet; urban patriciates of Bern, Zurich, Geneva (allied).
polities.religion: Catholic and Reformed cantons in armed coexistence—Calvin’s Geneva as Reformed beacon, central Swiss cantons as Catholic rock. Westphalia exteriorises a peace already practised as balance.
polities.culture: Alpine republican particularism; mercenary families; watchmaking and textile pockets; city print cultures in Basel, Zurich, Geneva (associate). Neutrality becomes a brand.
polities.summary: Armed confederation recognized independent at Westphalia, exporting mercenaries and guarding neutrality.

polities.name: Republic of Venice
polities.description: Venice still holds the terraferma, Dalmatian coasts, and (until the Cretan War’s end) Crete. Ottoman pressure and shifting trade routes erode the maritime empire; Morean War gains prove temporary. The oligarchic republic remains a distinct Italian power through 1789, museum-like and elegant, before French revolutionary armies end it in 1797. Candia’s twenty-four-year siege (to 1669) costs Crete; the Morean War briefly revives crusading memory under Francesco Morosini.
polities.conflicts: Cretan War (1645–69); Morean War (with temporary gains); later Ottoman wars; diplomatic tightrope among Spain, France, and Austria; French Revolutionary invasion ahead.
polities.leaders: Doges and patrician councils (Great Council, Senate, Council of Ten)—collective oligarchy.
polities.religion: Catholic with distinctive Venetian church privileges and suspicion of papal interference; Greek Orthodox subjects in overseas holdings; Jews in the Ghetto under supervised tolerance.
polities.culture: Carnival, opera, and tourism avant la lettre; lagoon print and glass; terraferma villa civilization (Palladian afterglow). Commerce shifts from spice empire to luxury services and regional trade.
polities.summary: Maritime oligarchy losing eastern empire to the Ottomans while staging opera, vedute, and Adriatic trade.
polities.story: Candia’s twenty-four-year siege (to 1669) costs Crete; the Morean War briefly revives crusading memory under Francesco Morosini. Canaletto’s views still sell a serene republic while the espionage state manages decline—until Bonaparte ends the Serenissima in 1797.
polities.literature: Sarpi’s anti-papal historiography earlier still shadows church-state pride; Goldoni’s comedies reform the stage; Casanova’s memoirs (later) mythologize the late republic; libretti for a city that invents public opera’s habits.
polities.art: Late Tintoretto/Veronese memory into Tiepolo’s airy ceilings; Canaletto and Guardi invent the veduta for Grand Tour buyers; carnival costume as civic art. Palladian villas inland remain the terraferma’s classical argument.
polities.ideas: Myth of Venice—mixed constitution praised by English republicans; Sarpi’s conciliar and anti-Jesuit strands; practical reason of state in Senate deliberations; quiet Quietist and libertine undercurrents in a censoring oligarchy.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Tuscany
polities.description: The Medici rule a mid-sized Italian grand duchy until Gian Gastone’s death (1737); Francis of Lorraine and then Peter Leopold bring Habsburg-secondary enlightened reform. Stable borders through 1789; Florence remains a capital of academies, galleries, and cautious modernization. Galileo’s Medici patronage is the duchy’s scientific origin myth—even as trial and house arrest follow.
polities.conflicts: War of the Spanish Succession orbit; War of the Polish Succession logistics; generally secondary Italian diplomacy rather than battlefield primacy.
polities.leaders: Cosimo II; Ferdinando II; Cosimo III; Gian Gastone; Francis Stephen; Peter Leopold (later Leopold II)—the reforming grand duke.
polities.religion: Catholic duchy; Leopoldine reform of church institutions, confraternities, and capital punishment (Tuscany famously moves against the death penalty in the 1780s).
polities.culture: Florentine academies and court science; Uffizi as dynastic gallery; Enlightenment reform under Peter Leopold making Tuscany a laboratory of Italian enlightened absolutism.
polities.summary: Medici then Habsburg-Lorraine grand duchy—Galileo’s patronage memory and Leopoldine reform laboratory.
polities.story: Galileo’s Medici patronage is the duchy’s scientific origin myth—even as trial and house arrest follow. The Medici line dies with Gian Gastone (1737); Lorraine-Habsburg rulers inherit a museum-state. Peter Leopold abolishes the death penalty (1786)—a Tuscan Enlightenment badge.
polities.literature: Academic prose and antiquarianism; Arcadian poetry; Beccaria’s On Crimes and Punishments as the era’s Tuscan-global intervention; travel guides selling Florence to the Grand Tour.
polities.art: Medici collecting becomes the Uffizi public myth; late baroque and neoclassical court commissions; peasant and villa landscapes of the contado. Dress follows French models more than Florentine pride.
polities.ideas: Galilean experimental philosophy; Accademia del Cimento’s programmed experiments; Beccaria’s influence on Leopoldine penal reform; physiocratic and legal Enlightenment.

polities.name: Duchy of Milan
polities.yearsActive: Spanish then Austrian Habsburg possession in this era
polities.description: Milan remains a rich Lombard possession: Spanish through the seventeenth century, Austrian after Utrecht. Governors extract revenue and hold a strategic hinge between Alps and peninsula. Maria Theresa and Joseph II introduce cadastral and legal reforms; the duchy is still Habsburg at 1789. Once Sforza, now a Spanish garrison jewel; plague of 1630 scars memory (Manzoni will later novelise it).
polities.conflicts: Franco-Spanish Italian echoes; War of the Spanish Succession; War of the Austrian Succession (French/Spanish occupation episodes); later coalition pressures.
polities.leaders: Spanish governors under Philip III/IV/Charles II; Austrian administrators under Charles VI, Maria Theresa, Joseph II; local patriciate in the Senate of Milan.
polities.religion: Catholic heartland with Borromean Counter-Reformation legacy—seminaries, confessionals, and disciplined parish life as Spanish then Austrian policy capitalise on Carlo Borromeo’s model.
polities.culture: Lombard urban wealth, silk, and finance; Spanish then Austrian court overlays; Enlightenment salons that will soon produce Verri and the Il Caffè circle.
polities.summary: Wealthy Lombard duchy under Spanish then Austrian Habsburgs; Borromean piety and Beccaria’s legal Enlightenment.
polities.story: Borromeo’s ghost still disciplines the city while Spanish governors treat it as a treasury. The Theresian cadastre tries to see every field for tax—an Enlightenment eye laid over a Renaissance economic engine—before French armies rewrite Italy again.
polities.literature: Legal and administrative Spanish/Italian prose; later Milanese Enlightenment journalism (Il Caffè); theatrical life feeding Vienna and Paris tastes.
polities.art: Duomo’s long building site; Spanish walls; baroque churches; later neoclassical projects under Austria. Painting schools less globally famous than Venice/Rome yet tied to rich confraternities.
polities.ideas: Borromean pastoral reform as applied theology; Cesare Beccaria’s On Crimes and Punishments (1764) from the Milanese Enlightenment; Verri brothers’ Il Caffè journal.

polities.name: Papal States
polities.description: The Papal States stretch across Lazio, Umbria, Marche, and Romagna as the pope’s temporal monarchy. Nepotism softens into more bureaucratic congregations; finances wobble; artistic patronage still sets Catholic Europe’s taste. The states survive Italian wars into 1789, soon to face revolutionary and Napoleonic storms. Urban VIII’s Barberini bees mark a peak of nepotism and building; Bernini shapes St Peter’s square into an embrace of stone.
polities.conflicts: War of Castro memory; alignments in the Spanish Succession; Corsican and Italian diplomatic crises; later French Revolutionary pressure and eventual 1798 republic ahead.
polities.leaders: Popes from Clement VIII through Urban VIII, Innocent X, and on to Pius VI in this span; cardinal-nephews as power brokers.
polities.religion: Catholic theocracy and Tridentine reform centre—Index, Inquisition, jubilees, and the curia as Europe’s confessional supreme court, even as philosophes mock and Catholic monarchs practise regalism.
polities.culture: Rome as pilgrimage, court, and academy city; multilingual clerical elites; antiquarian digging that feeds European classicism. Temporal misrule myths circulate beside genuine artistic magnetism.
polities.summary: Temporal papal monarchy whose Baroque Rome stages Catholic Europe’s art and curial politics.
polities.story: Urban VIII’s Barberini bees mark a peak of nepotism and building; Bernini shapes St Peter’s square into an embrace of stone. The temporal state lags economically while spiritually staging Catholicism for the world—Pius VI still tours as a baroque sovereign on the eve of revolutionary shock.
polities.literature: Latin bulls and vernacular devotionals; Barberini and later academy poetry; guidebooks to churches and ruins; Muratori-style antiquarianism influencing Catholic reform thought.
polities.art: High baroque apex—Bernini’s colonnade and ecstasies, Borromini’s geometries, Cortona ceilings; then rococo softness and neoclassical reaction in museums. Dress of cardinals as color-coded power.
polities.ideas: Tridentine theology institutionalised; Bellarmine’s afterlife; Quietism controversies; anti-Jansenist politics; late scholastic resistance to Enlightenment natural religion.

polities.description: The Kingdom of Naples under Spanish viceroys (Sicily often linked) is one of Europe’s most populous Italian realms. Masaniello’s 1647 revolt scars the century; after the Succession War the realm passes briefly to Austria before Bourbon conquest. Mapped to 1700; later ticks use the Two Sicilies layer. polities.leaders: Spanish viceroys under Philip III/IV/Charles II; local barons; Masaniello as popular tribune.
polities.religion: Intense baroque Catholicism—saints, processions, San Gennaro’s blood miracle as civic theology; strong clerical and confraternity presence beside popular syncretic habits.
polities.culture: Naples as a mega-city of music (conservatories), law, and street theatre; latifundia interiors; Spanish court ceremony over Greek-Roman-medieval layers.
polities.summary: Spanish Habsburg viceroyalty of southern Italy—vast city, baronial countryside, baroque faith.
polities.story: In 1647 a fisherman, Masaniello, briefly tops a tax revolt that becomes a European news event; Spain reasserts control. The kingdom remains a Spanish fiscal milch-cow until the Succession war reshuffles Italy—and Bourbon ambition remakes the south afterward.
polities.literature: Dialect theatre and chronicles of revolt; legal scholarship; Giambattista Basile’s fairy-tale Pentamerone earlier still echoing; sacred oratory.
polities.art: Neapolitan Baroque painting (Ribera’s Spanish-Neapolitan school); compact sacred architecture; street presepe culture; musical conservatories feeding European opera.

polities.name: Republic of Genoa
polities.description: Genoa persists as a Ligurian maritime republic with a banking aristocracy and a restless Corsican possession sold to France in 1768 after Paoli’s revolts. Mediterranean trade and credit sustain a small political footprint through 1789; Napoleonic extinction lies ahead. Bankers who once funded Spain watch their Mediterranean horizon shrink.
polities.conflicts: Corsican revolts under Pasquale Paoli; French pressure; Austrian and Spanish naval entanglements; later Napoleonic end (1797).
polities.leaders: Doges of the oligarchic republic; Bank of Saint George elites; Paoli in Corsica.
polities.religion: Catholic; Jesuit and later reformed educational fights similar to other Italian states.
polities.culture: Mercantile aristocracy of the Strade Nuove palaces; Corsican clan and republican resistance culture; silk and credit instruments as Genoa’s quieter empire.
polities.summary: Ligurian oligarchic republic—banking memory, Corsican headache, shrinking footprint.
polities.story: Bankers who once funded Spain watch their Mediterranean horizon shrink. Corsica’s long revolt ends with sale to France (1768)—Paoli’s island republic becomes a European cause célèbre, and Napoleon is born a French subject the next year.
polities.literature: Corsican political writing and Paoli’s republican fame in European letters (Boswell); Genoese administrative prose; travel accounts of the riviera.
polities.art: Rubens/Van Dyck earlier Genoese portrait clients’ palaces still define the Strade Nuove; late baroque churches; maritime votive paintings.
polities.ideas: Oligarchic republicanism without Dutch-style popular myth; Corsican resistance ideology admired by Rousseauists; credit and asiento memory as economic thought-in-practice.
