polities.name: Savoy / Kingdom of Sardinia
polities.yearsActive: Duchy of Savoy; Kingdom of Sardinia from 1720
polities.description: The House of Savoy plays great-power wars with deft side-switching. Victor Amadeus II gains Sicily then swaps for Sardinia and a royal title (1720). By 1750–1789 the state spans Piedmont, Savoy, Nice, and Sardinia—a compact military-absolutist kingdom centered on Turin, poised for later Risorgimento fame. Victor Amadeus II trades sides in the Spanish Succession and walks away with a crown (Sardinia, 1720).
polities.conflicts: Thirty Years’ War orbit; War of the Spanish Succession (key Alpine theatres); War of the Austrian Succession; later Revolutionary wars. Waldensian valleys as internal confessional wound.
polities.leaders: Charles Emmanuel I; Victor Amadeus II; Charles Emmanuel III; Victor Amadeus III. Bureaucrats building the Piedmontese file-state.
polities.religion: Catholic state with Waldensian minority under periodic persecution and later limited toleration—Alpine confessional frontier.
polities.culture: Turin military-absolutist court; French and Italian bilingual administration; alpine fortress society; Sardinian distinctiveness under mainland kings.
polities.summary: Alpine buffer that trades sides in the Succession wars and emerges as the Kingdom of Sardinia.
polities.story: Victor Amadeus II trades sides in the Spanish Succession and walks away with a crown (Sardinia, 1720). The duchy becomes a kingdom that drills, maps, and waits—later the nucleus of Italian unification, already a disciplined Alpine machine by 1789.
polities.literature: Court and legal Italian/French; later Alfieri ( Piedmont-born) will rage against tyrants off this tick’s end; administrative memorials as the genre of state-building.
polities.art: Juvarra’s and Guarini’s architecture in Turin and Piedmont; baroque hunting palaces; military engineering as aesthetic of power; alpine sacred mounts (Sacri Monti).
polities.ideas: Absolute ducal/royal sovereignty on a small stage; anti-Waldensian confessional politics; reason-of-state manuals for buffer kingdoms between Bourbon and Habsburg.

polities.name: Crimean Khanate
polities.description: The Crimean Khanate controls the peninsula and projects cavalry power across the Black Sea steppe, raiding and trading slaves while serving as Ottoman sword-arm against Poland-Lithuania and Russia. Catherine II annexes Crimea in 1783; the polity is absent at the 1789 tick. For centuries the khanate’s cavalry is the Ottoman northern claw.
polities.conflicts: Russo-Crimean wars; campaigns as Ottoman vassal against Habsburgs and Commonwealth; internal Giray succession strife; final Russian annexation warpath (1783).
polities.leaders: Giray khans under Ottoman oversight; notable late figures facing Russian pressure before 1783.
polities.religion: Sunni Islam with steppe customary overlays; mosques and madrasas in Bakhchysarai; Christian and Jewish minorities in coastal trading towns.
polities.culture: Tatar steppe khanate culture linking Nogai grasslands to Ottoman courts; Bakhchysarai palace life; slave trade and horse economy; multilingual diplomacy (Turkic, Ottoman, Slavic).
polities.summary: Giray Tatar khanate under Ottoman suzerainty—steppe cavalry power until Russian annexation (1783).
polities.story: For centuries Moscow paid and prayed against Crimean raids; by Catherine’s reign the balance reverses and the khanate is swallowed—Black Sea access becoming Russian strategic dogma. The fountain of Bakhchysarai later romanticizes what empire erased.
polities.literature: Turkic chronicles and oral epic; Ottoman chancery correspondence; later European captivity narratives that exoticize the khanate even as it falls.
polities.art: Bakhchysarai palace ornament; Islamic calligraphy and metalwork; steppe tent aesthetics beside stone mosques; Crimean port hybridities at Kaffa/Feodosia.
polities.ideas: Chinggisid Giray legitimacy under Islamic Ottoman suzerainty—a dual political theology; steppe customary law beside sharia courts; pragmatic vassalage as survival strategy.

polities.name: Principality of Wallachia
polities.description: Wallachia remains a distinct tributary principality under Ottoman suzerainty, ruled by native dynasts and, from the early eighteenth century, Phanariot hospodars appointed through Istanbul. Caught among Ottoman, Habsburg, and Russian pressures, it keeps a mapped identity through 1789. Constantin Brâncoveanu’s careful diplomacy ends in Istanbul execution (1714); the Phanariot century follows—Greek-speaking princes farming taxes for the Porte while Orthodox culture persists in monasteries along the Carpathians and Danube.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman–Habsburg wars on its borders; Russian interventions; episodic anti-Ottoman risings; boyar factional violence. Military traffic more than sovereign campaigning.
polities.leaders: Native dynasts (e.g. Brâncoveanu at the era’s hinge); Phanariot hospodars from the early eighteenth century appointed via Istanbul.
polities.religion: Eastern Orthodox principality—monasteries as landholders and culture banks under the Ecumenical Patriarchate’s wider orbit.
polities.culture: Romanian Orthodox princely culture; boyar estate society; Slavic-Romanian liturgical inheritance shifting toward Romanian cultural assertiveness; Phanariot Greek overlay in the 1700s.
polities.summary: Orthodox Danubian principality under Ottoman suzerainty, later under Phanariot hospodars.
polities.story: Constantin Brâncoveanu’s martyrdom under Ottoman suspicion (1714) becomes a founding trauma; Phanariot rule afterward turns Bucharest into a bilingual court of Greek letters and Romanian peasantry—autonomy as a negotiated performance before the sultan.
polities.literature: Chronicles of the princes; religious translations into Romanian; Greek Phanariot learning; boyar memorials. Oral ballad memory of outlaw and frontier figures.
polities.art: Brâncovenesc church architecture mixing Ottoman, Byzantine, and local forms; monastery frescoes; princely courts at Bucharest and Târgoviște; boyar costume as rank script.
polities.ideas: Orthodox political theology of the prince as church protector under infidel suzerainty; boyar customary law; Phanariot administrative rationalism imported from the Phanar.

polities.name: Principality of Moldavia
polities.description: Moldavia mirrors Wallachia as an Orthodox tributary principality, with stronger Polish and later Russian entanglement. Phanariot hospodars dominate the eighteenth century; Austria annexes Bukovina in 1775 while the core remains Ottoman-vassal at 1789. Moldavia is a corridor state: Polish magnates, Ottoman tribute, and Russian ‘protection’ take turns.
polities.conflicts: Polish, Ottoman, and Russian wars across Moldavian land; Hotin fortress wars; Habsburg annexation of Bukovina; boyar coups around the throne.
polities.leaders: Native princes including early Movilă lines; Phanariot hospodars in the eighteenth century.
polities.religion: Eastern Orthodox—with monasteries (including later-famous northern Moldavian painted churches’ heritage) anchoring identity under Ottoman tribute.
polities.culture: Romanian Orthodox culture with Polish diplomatic habits; Iași as princely capital; Jewish and Armenian trading diasporas; Phanariot Greek overlay.
polities.summary: Eastern Carpathian Orthodox vassal between Poland, Ottomans, and Russia; Bukovina lost to Austria in 1775.
polities.story: Dimitrie Cantemir’s brief Russian alliance and exile scholarship (Descriptio Moldaviae) show a prince trying to think the land into European knowledge while losing the throne. Bukovina’s 1775 loss to Austria teaches that vassal buffers are partitionable long before 1789.
polities.literature: Cantemir’s Latin and Romanian works bridging Ottoman and European learning; chronicles; religious translation; Greek court letters under Phanariots.
polities.art: Painted monastery tradition of northern Moldavia as living sacred art; princely courts at Iași; liturgical embroidery; wooden vernacular architecture.
polities.ideas: Cantemir’s humanist-Orthodox encyclopedism; boyar constitutional customs; Phanariot administrative thought; awareness of being a hinge among three empires.
